Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

purpose noun

what something is for, the aim

also aim, for the purpose of, in order to, so as to, what for?, what’s the point?, intention, the point of

classical

Liv. 5.27.2: lūsūs exercendīque causā
Plin. Ep. 9.36.3: nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī

causā (+ genitive)

ablative of causa, placed after a genitive: a noun, a gerund or a gerundive

for the purpose of, for the sake of

Lewis & Short: in the best prose “almost always referring to the future, and implying a purpose”. For “on purpose” see mean (intend): cōnsultō.

Other words

  • ut, nē (+ subjunctive) — in order to, so that (not)

    conjunction, with the subjunctive; nē for a purpose to be avoided · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.42: ēnītī et contendere dēbet quam maximē possit, ut vincat; Caes. BG 1.48: eō cōnsiliō utī frūmentō commeātūque … Caesarem interclūderet

    The commonest way to state a purpose: Latin uses a clause where English uses the noun (vēnī ut tē vidērem, the purpose of my visit was to see you). After verbs of going, the supine in -um: lūsum it, he goes off to play (Hor. S. 1.5.48).

  • cōnsilium, cōnsiliī n. — a purpose, an intention: what someone means to do

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.48: eō cōnsiliō utī frūmentō commeātūque … Caesarem interclūderet; Ter. Eun. 1024: quā spē aut quō cōnsiliō hūc īmus?

    Eō cōnsiliō ut, with the purpose of; quō cōnsiliō?, for what purpose? Also a decision and advice (see decision).

  • fīnis, fīnis m. — the end a thing serves, its purpose

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.138: domum … cujus fīnis est ūsus; Quint. 2.17.22: omnēs artēs habēre fīnem aliquem prōpositum, ad quem tendunt (Lewis & Short)

    Of the purpose a thing exists for; a person’s own aim is rather cōnsilium or prōpositum (Lewis & Short).

  • quōrsum? — to what end? what for?

    adverb, interrogative · also used · classical · Hor. S. 2.7.116: quōrsum est opus?; Cic. Leg. 1.4: quōrsum tandem aut cūr ista quaeris?

    Lewis & Short: “to what purpose? to what end? with what view? for what?”; quōrsus, inquam, istuc?, what are you getting at? (Cic. Brut. 292, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • is cum in pāce īnstituisset puerōs ante urbem lūsūs exercendīque causā prōdūcere

    he had made it his practice in peacetime to take the boys out in front of the city for play and exerciseLiv. 5.27.2

  • ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō

    I read a speech in Greek or Latin aloud and with energy, not so much for the sake of my voice as of my digestionPlin. Ep. 9.36.3

  • lūsum it Maecēnās, dormītum ego Vergiliusque

    Maecenas goes off to play ball, Virgil and I to sleepHor. S. 1.5.48

  • ‘unde mihi lapidem?’ ‘quōrsum est opus?’ ‘unde sagittās?’

    ‘Where can I get a stone?’ ‘What do you need it for?’ ‘Where can I get arrows?’Hor. S. 2.7.116

See also mean, reason, plan, decision.
